n: The chronicler returns to Judah’s clans with a quick line of descent from Judah through several generations. These names lead into additional family branches not covered in chapter 2.

f.g: Probably a copying variant for Caleb (Chelubai) in 2:9, since Carmi belonged to Zerah’s line.

n: These families settled around Zorah in the lowlands west of Jerusalem.

f.g: People of Zorah, Samson’s hometown (Judges 13:2).

n: The founders of Etam are listed, including a daughter with an unusual name. Etam was later fortified by King Rehoboam.

f.g: A rare woman’s name, perhaps meaning “give shade, you who turn toward me.”

n: Hur’s descendants founded towns in the Judean hills, and Hur himself is linked with Bethlehem’s founding.
Ashur, founder of Tekoa, had two wives whose sons are listed next.
The sons of Naarah. Haahashtari may be a clan name rather than a personal name.

f.g: Possibly “the Ahashtarite,” a clan with a Persian-sounding name.

n: The sons of Helah, Ashur’s other wife.

f.g: Means “gift” or “hire.”

n: More clans of Judah, whose connection to the main line is not spelled out—the chronicler preserves even the names he cannot fully place.

f.g: Ancestor of a clan; the name may mean “thorn.”

n: Suddenly the list pauses for a story. Jabez was more honorable than his brothers, yet his name sounds like the Hebrew word for “pain,” given because of his difficult birth.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew ‘otsev, “pain” or “sorrow”—a name that could feel like a curse.
More respected, or of better character.

n: Jabez prays that God will bless him, widen his land, be with him, and keep him from harm so his name would not define his life. God answers. The lesson: no one’s past or label is beyond God’s power to bless.

f.g: Expand my territory; “coast” in the KJV means border or region.

f.w: God granted him that which he requested

n: The genealogy resumes with the clan of Chelub.

f.g: Another form of the name Caleb, though perhaps a different person.

n: These families settled at towns like Ir-nahash, “city of the serpent,” possibly a copper-working site.

f.g: “City of the snake” or “city of copper”; location uncertain.

n: Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, was Israel’s first judge after Joshua, who delivered Israel from oppression and brought forty years of peace.
Joab (not David’s general) founded the “valley of craftsmen,” a community known for skilled work.

f.g: “Craftsmen”; the valley of skilled workers.

n: The family of Caleb son of Jephunneh—the faithful spy who, with Joshua, trusted God to give Israel the land and received Hebron as his inheritance.
The sons of Jehaleleel, whose names include Ziph, a town in Judah’s wilderness.
The sons of Ezra (an ancestor, not the later scribe), including a daughter named Miriam—the same name as Moses’ sister.

f.g: Here possibly a son or daughter; the Hebrew is unclear. The name is the source of “Mary.”

n: Mered had a Judahite wife and an Egyptian wife, Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh. A foreign princess joined Israel’s family—God’s covenant people have always welcomed outsiders.

f.g: Her name means “daughter of the LORD,” perhaps given after she joined Israel.
“The Jewess,” probably meaning his Judahite wife.

n: The sons of Hodiah are tied to Keilah, a town David later rescued from the Philistines.
Two more short family lists from Judah.

f.g: “Son of the gracious one.”

n: Judah’s third son Shelah had descendants who became a guild of linen weavers—Chronicles remembers people by their trades as well as their names.

f.g: Made fine linen cloth, a valued skill.

n: Some of Shelah’s clans once ruled in Moab. The chronicler notes these are “ancient things”—old records he faithfully preserved.

f.g: These records are very old, a hint that the chronicler drew on earlier sources.

n: These families were royal potters and gardeners, living on crown estates to work for the king.

f.g: Possibly place names, Netaim and Gederah, or simply farmland and enclosures.

n: The tribe of Simeon is introduced next. Simeon’s land lay within Judah’s territory in the south, and over time the two tribes largely merged.
Simeon’s line continues through Shaul’s descendants.

f.g: “Sweet smell”; a name also found among Ishmael’s sons (1 Chronicles 1:29).

n: Three more generations lead to Shimei.

f.g: Related to the name Zacchaeus, meaning “remembered.”

n: Shimei had a large family, but Simeon as a whole stayed small compared with Judah—fulfilling Jacob’s words that Simeon would be scattered.

f.w: neither did all their family multiply

n: Simeon’s towns in the Negev, the dry southern region, begin with Beer-sheba, famous from the stories of Abraham and Isaac.
More of Simeon’s southern towns.

f.g: Called Balah in Joshua 19:3.

n: These towns include Hormah, site of an early victory, and Ziklag, which later became David’s base while fleeing Saul.
Simeon held these towns until David’s reign, when they apparently came under Judah’s control.

f.g: Until David’s time, when Judah absorbed much of Simeon’s territory.

n: Simeon also held five villages, including Rimmon and Ashan.
The chronicler notes that these settlements, together with their surrounding villages, were Simeon’s officially recorded homes.

f.g: Dwelling places.

n: A list of Simeonite clan leaders begins.

f.g: Not King Amaziah; a clan leader of Simeon.

n: More leaders, several traced back four generations.

f.g: A common name; not the king of Israel.

n: Still more Simeonite leaders, among them Jaakobah, a form of Jacob.

f.g: A form of the name Jacob.

n: Ziza’s ancestry is traced back five generations, showing the care taken to record family lines.

f.g: A leader of Simeon; the name may mean “abundance.”

n: These men were leaders of their clans, and their families grew so large that they needed more land.

f.g: Clan chiefs or family heads.

n: Looking for grazing land, they moved toward Gedor.

f.g: Possibly to be read “Gerar,” a region in the southwest near Philistia, as in the Greek translation.

n: They found rich, peaceful pastureland once occupied by descendants of Ham—perhaps Egyptians or Canaanites.

f.g: Peoples descended from Ham, such as Egyptians or Canaanites (1 Chronicles 1:8).

n: In Hezekiah’s time these Simeonites drove out the residents and settled there. The chronicler records this without approving or condemning it.

f.w: in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah
f.g: About 715–686 BC.
Lived in their place.

n: Five hundred Simeonites went southeast to the hills of Seir, the region of Edom.

f.g: The mountainous region of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea.

n: There they defeated the last surviving Amalekites, Israel’s ancient enemies, and settled in their place.

f.w: the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped
